newsitem.title: USA: U.S. troops prepare for possible Zaire evacuation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. troops prepare for possible Zaire evacuation.

text.p: The United States is sending hundreds of troops to West Africa to prepare for the possible emergency evacuation of Americans from Zaire, although no order to do so has been issued, the Pentagon said on Friday.
The U.S. forces will join French troops and planes already in nearby Gabon and Congo in case evacuations from strife-torn Zaire become necessary.

"The Department of Defence has directed the U.S. European Command to deploy enabling forces, consisting of several hundred personnel, as part of contingency planning for a possible future evacuation from Zaire," the Pentagon said in a written statement issued late on Friday.
"This deployment does not represent a U.S. commitment to any particular course of action," it added.

The Pentagon gave no details about the preparations but said the troops included command-and-support elements for a forward joint task force primarily from the United States military base in Vicenza, Italy, supplemented with personnel from some domestic units. It will be led by Army Maj. Gen. Edwin Smith, Commander Southern European Task Force.
"This deployment represents an enhancement to planning for contingency measures to ensure the security of U.S. citizens in Zaire if an evacuation should become necessary," the Pentagon said.

U.S. task force units will go to locations in several West African countries, including Brazzaville, Republic of Congo and Libreville, Republic of Gabon. A few task force members could visit Zaire "if that becomes necessary as part of the planning process," the Pentagon said.
U.S. officials on Friday were monitoring the civil strife in Zaire hour-by-hour to assess whether to evacuate some 650 Americans, but had received no request to do so from the embassy in Kinshasa.
The State Department announced a new warning to U.S. citizens to defer travel to Zaire and strongly encouraged dependents of U.S. Embassy personnel in Kinshasa to depart.
The warning was issued "due to the uncertain political and security situation and the potential for unrest throughout the country," the State Department said.
France has advised its citizens to leave Zaire and has moved aircraft and about 100 troops to be ready for any evacuation.

A 30-member U.S. military team was sent to the central African state on Wednesday to monitor the situation and the possible use of roads, airfields and communications in any emergency movement of Americans.
"We are in the preparatorial stage to make sure we can act if action is called for," U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen told reporters.

When asked if he believed evacuation would be needed, Cohen said "that depends on a day-by-day assessment, it could be an hour-by-hour assessment, that we are following very closely and as usual we will take every measure possible to make sure our citizens are safe."
Rebels who have been fighting since October 1996 to topple Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko seized the key city of Kisangani last weekend.

Mobutu left France where he had undergone cancer treatment and returned home on Friday in an effort to salvage control of the Central African country. But Laurent Kabila's rebels rejected a call for a ceasefire followed by peace negotiations. "We negotiate first," Kabila said on arrival in Kisangani.
